name: Maya Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What do you do on a normal building-site day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three and lead a carpentry crew making temporary timber forms before concrete is poured. The trade certificate gave me the rules, and experience tells me when a brace feels wrong. I use AI every day to compare drawings and count panels, then walk the whole form before anyone pours. I am paid above the usual rate; my partner and I have two schoolchildren, a mortgage and more than six months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a quicker panel count is welcome, but the crew still has to brace the form correctly. An AI panel count cannot hold wet concrete inside a weak building form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my higher wage and lead role to hold. We have a long savings runway and plenty of builders nearby, so I can use a helpful tool without fearing for this month’s mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading formwork and use my daily AI drawing check as usual. I would walk the braces and sign off the physical form before a pour, even if the list comes back perfect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this small change. Counting faster is useful, but it does not alter the safety duty on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the last thing you check before a pour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The brace connections and where pressure will push the panels. I ask someone else to look at the opposite side too, because a tidy list cannot show a loose fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you learn anything new from this small change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I already use the drawing and count tool daily; this picture does not call for a new AI skill.

say: I would **use** AI for panel counts and still inspect every brace before a pour.
I would **tell** the crew physical sign-off stays with us.
think: My **lead** role, good wage and long savings runway look safe.
**Daily** AI use is already familiar, not a fresh training plan.
do: **Keep** leading formwork and physically checking braces before concrete pours.
**Continue** existing daily AI drawing and panel counts.
feel: **Calm** about secure work and household finances.
S0.quote: An AI panel count cannot hold wet concrete inside a weak building form.
fieldNote: **Maya** uses AI daily but treats physical formwork inspection as a separate safety duty.
**Higher** wages, savings beyond six months and many nearby builders support calm when only routine counts change.

steps.text: Keep leading and physically inspecting site formwork

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that smarter buying and planning could give us fewer missing panels. I would learn the new AI pour-sequencing feature early, but I would test it against a completed form and our paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think management could schedule tighter pours and cut paid preparation time. My higher basic wage and savings protect the mortgage, but my crew’s hours and my own overtime could realistically shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use one completed job to train on the sequencing feature, then compare it with two live pours. I would ask the builder for written crew-hour targets and keep checking bracing before any concrete arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about possible paid-hour cuts, though I have savings and skill to bargain with. An AI pour schedule cannot turn an unpaid brace check into a safe one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would fail your test of the new feature?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A sequence that sends concrete before the final brace check. I would stop that pour and show the planner the site record, whatever the computer says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the builder says fewer preparation hours are enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the new rate and safety time in writing. If the paid hours truly shrink, I would compare posted local lead jobs at wages that cover mortgage and school bills.

say: I would **learn** new pour-sequencing controls and test them against real forms.
I would **insist** on paid time for the physical brace check.
think: **Tighter** scheduling could reduce my overtime and the crew’s wages.
**Savings** help, but they do not make an unsafe unpaid rush acceptable.
do: **Learn** new AI sequencing controls on completed and live formwork jobs.
**Ask** builder for written paid preparation time and safety checks.
**Compare** posted local lead vacancies at household-covering pay if hours shrink.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible paid-hour loss, with strong options.
S1.quote: An AI pour schedule cannot turn an unpaid brace check into a safe one.
fieldNote: She **learns** new AI controls proactively and tests against site safety and actual paid hours.
**Potential** overtime and crew-hour cuts justify anxiety despite her strong savings and higher base pay.

steps.text: Learn new AI pour-sequencing controls on actual formwork
Keep paid site work while checking written safety hours
Compare posted local lead jobs at household-covering pay after hour cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI in 2028, when I am forty-five, can design a form but cannot lift a panel. Around 2031, when I am forty-eight, capable hands-on robots could assemble the standard forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own paid formwork hours could shrink if the builder buys those robots. We have more than six months saved and plenty of local builders, but I would want an actual safe checking role rather than a grand promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a paid, supervised trial of robot-built formwork, with a human signing the brace inspection before a pour. If my hours fell after robots arrived, I would apply to posted local site-safety jobs only if the pay covers our mortgage and children’s costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real hours risk, yet able to act. I have the savings to reject an unsafe or poorly paid offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you refuse to sign in that trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A form whose bracing was hidden behind panels before I checked the fixings. A robot may build the timber form, but wet concrete still tests every brace I sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave a well-paid crew now for a safety title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a posted local role with a clear bill-covering wage and actual inspection authority. I would not resign for a title without those conditions.

say: **Thinking** AI reaches drawings in 2028; robots may assemble forms around 2031.
I would **demand** a paid supervised trial and human safety sign-off.
think: My **paid** fitting hours might shrink, but savings and nearby builders give choices.
A **safety** role needs real inspection authority, a posted local place and household-covering wages.
do: **Request** paid supervised robot-form trial with human brace sign-off before pours.
**Keep** paid formwork shifts while trial runs.
**Apply** after hour cuts to posted local safety job at household-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about possible own-hour loss, with financial and job options.
S2.quote: A robot may build the timber form, but wet concrete still tests every brace I sign.
fieldNote: Her **adaptive** response is a paid supervised trial with a specific brace inspection and stop-work condition.
She **preserves** the sequence from 2028 thinking work to 2031 physical robots and requires a real adequate local role.

steps.text: Keep paid formwork if requested supervised robot safety trial runs
Apply after cuts to posted local safety job with bill-covering wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am forty-eight, with capable site robots around 2034 when I am fifty-one. The extra years let me qualify for formal formwork inspection before robot-built forms are common.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want that credential, but only if the builder funds the course, pays the study days and a suitable local vacancy is posted. My savings give me room to choose, not a reason to subsidise an employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading paid formwork and enroll in a funded, paid-time structural inspection course once a posted local role with adequate wages is in view. After qualifying I would apply to that posted job, provided it pays enough for the mortgage and school costs and gives me real safety sign-off authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about a later transition and anxious if fitting hours are cut. Five years gives me time to match training with a genuine job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course teach beyond your daily checks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Formal load and sign-off records for temporary forms, not just the practical brace check. A robot formwork inspector needs permission to stop a concrete pour, not just a certificate on a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the builder funds the course but will not pay the study days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on my paid crew role and seek another funded paid-time offer. The saving account is for our family, not free labour for training.

say: The 2031 **thinking** change precedes formwork robots around 2034.
I would **complete** formal inspection training only with funding, paid time and a posted suitable local role.
think: **Practical** formwork checks need a formal credential for independent sign-off.
A **posted** job must offer real safety authority and household-covering wages.
do: **Enroll** in funded paid-time structural inspection course for posted suitable local role.
**Keep** leading paid formwork until a qualifying offer exists.
**Apply** after qualification to posted local safety role with authority and adequate pay.
feel: **Anxious** if fitting hours fall, with a conditional five-year route.
S3.quote: A robot formwork inspector needs permission to stop a concrete pour, not just a certificate on a wall.
fieldNote: Her **route** includes actual enrollment, later application and authority to stop unsafe work.
**Course** funding, paid time, a posted local vacancy and adequate salary remain distinct conditions.

steps.text: Enroll in funded paid-time inspection course for posted suitable local role
Keep paid formwork until qualifying offer
Apply after qualification to posted local safety role with authority and adequate pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am fifty-three, and capable formwork robots around 2039 when I am fifty-six. A decade would let me test tools carefully and save more of my higher wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the crew and my income to stay sound for years. I could eventually move into paid training or inspection, but I need a funded course on paid time and a posted local role with proper safety authority and enough salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading safe forms, add new money from each paid quarter to the mortgage reserve, and practice new AI site-record controls as they appear. If a funded paid-time inspection course and posted adequate local job emerge, I would complete the course and apply after qualifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few years and curious about the longer change. A decade before formwork robots lets me build a better savings account without guessing which machine wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which new AI control would you practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A site-record feature that links the measured brace location to a photograph and inspection time. I would test it on a finished form before relying on it during a pour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would teaching appeal if an opening appeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if it were a posted local paid role that covered our bills and let me teach safe formwork. I would not leave a good wage for an informal invitation.

say: A **decade** lets me test new site records and add new wages to savings.
I would **require** real safety authority and adequate local pay before changing roles.
think: The **current** good wage and strong savings make the next years secure.
**Later** training must be funded on paid time and linked to a posted job.
do: **Save** new money from paid formwork quarters after household bills.
**Learn** new AI site-record controls on finished forms before live pours.
**Complete** funded paid-time inspection course for posted adequate local safety job.
feel: **Calm** about near-term work and curious about tested tools.
S4.quote: A decade before formwork robots lets me build a better savings account without guessing which machine wins.
fieldNote: Her **adaptive** stance includes actual practice with new AI site-record controls and fresh saving from wages.
**Any** formal course or move stays tied to funding, paid hours, a posted local job, adequate salary and safety authority.

steps.text: Save new pay from formwork quarters after bills
Learn new AI site-record controls on finished forms
Complete funded paid-time inspection course for posted adequate local safety job
Apply after qualification to posted local safety role with authority and household-covering pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028/2031 case concerns me most because my formwork hours could shrink before a safe robot checking role is real. A paid supervised trial, written safety authority and a posted local job at adequate wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who can stop a pour when a robot has fitted the form. I would rather lose an hour opening a panel than sign a brace I could not see. No digital drawing can take responsibility for concrete pushing against a hidden timber brace.

headlineQuote: No digital drawing can take responsibility for concrete pushing against a hidden timber brace.
portrait: **Maya** is a forty-three-year-old trade-certified lead carpenter who builds temporary forms before concrete pours.
Her **higher** wage, savings beyond six months, mortgage, schoolchildren and many nearby builders give options.
She **uses** AI daily and learns new site-record tools early while demanding physical safety proof.
A **later** move requires funded paid training, a posted local adequate job and real authority to stop unsafe pours.
biggestWorry: **Fast** robots around 2031 could reduce paid formwork hours before a safe checking role exists.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid** supervised trial, written stop-work authority and a posted local role at household-covering wages would help.
